title: Chapter 8 — The Federal Constitution
paragraphs: Up to this point I have considered each State as a separate whole, and I have explained the different springs the people sets in motion and the different means of action it employs. But all the States I have treated as independent are forced, in certain cases, to submit to the supreme authority of the Union. The time has come to examine separately the supremacy with which the Union has been invested, and to cast a rapid glance over the Federal Constitution.
Origin of the first Union — Its weakness — Congress appeals to the constituent authority — Interval of two years between this appeal and the promulgation of the new Constitution.
History of the Federal Constitution

The thirteen colonies that simultaneously threw off the yoke of England toward the end of the last century professed, as I have already observed, the same religion, the same language, the same customs, and almost the same laws. They were struggling against a common enemy, and these reasons were strong enough to unite them to one another and to consolidate them into a single nation. But since each had enjoyed a separate existence and a government of its own, the particular interests and customs that resulted from this system stood in the way of the close and intimate union that would have absorbed each State’s individual importance into the general importance of all. Hence arose two opposite tendencies, one prompting the Anglo-Americans to unite, the other to divide their strength. As long as the war with the mother country lasted, necessity kept the principle of union alive, and though the laws that constituted it were defective, the common tie held in spite of its imperfections. *a But no sooner was peace concluded than the defects of the legislation became manifest, and the State seemed suddenly dissolved. Each colony became an independent republic and assumed absolute sovereignty. The federal government, condemned to impotence by its constitution and no longer sustained by the presence of a common danger, watched the great nations of Europe insult its flag while it was scarcely able to hold its ground against the Indian tribes and to pay the interest on the debt contracted during the war of independence. It was already on the verge of destruction when it officially declared its inability to govern and appealed to the constituent authority of the nation. *b If America ever approached (however briefly) that lofty pinnacle of glory to which the imagination of its inhabitants is wont to point, it was at the solemn moment when the power of the nation, as it were, abdicated its rule over the land. Every age has furnished the spectacle of a people struggling energetically to win its independence, and the efforts of the Americans in throwing off the English yoke have been considerably exaggerated. Separated from their enemies by three thousand miles of ocean and backed by a powerful ally, the success of the United States may more justly be attributed to their geographical position than to the valor of their armies or the patriotism of their citizens. It would be ridiculous to compare the American war to the wars of the French Revolution, or the efforts of the Americans to those of the French when they were attacked by the whole of Europe, without credit and without allies, and yet capable of opposing a twentieth part of their population to the world and of carrying the torch of revolution beyond their frontiers while they smothered its devouring flame at home. But it is a novelty in the history of society to see a great people turn a calm and scrutinizing eye on itself when informed by the legislature that the wheels of government have stopped; to see it carefully examine the extent of the evil, and patiently wait two whole years until a remedy was discovered, which it voluntarily adopted without wringing a tear or a drop of blood from mankind. When the inadequacy of the first constitution was discovered, America possessed the double advantage of the calm that had succeeded the excitement of the revolution, and of those great men who had led the revolution to a successful issue. The assembly that accepted the task of composing the second constitution was small, *c but George Washington was its President, and it contained the choicest talents and the noblest hearts that had ever appeared in the New World. This national commission, after long and careful deliberation, offered to the acceptance of the people the body of general laws that still rules the Union. All the States adopted it successively. *d The new Federal Government began its functions in 1789, after an interregnum of two years. The American Revolution ended when the French Revolution began.

a [ See the articles of the first confederation formed in 1778. This constitution was not adopted by all the States until 1781. See also the analysis given of this constitution in “The Federalist” from No. 15 to No. 22, inclusive, and Story’s “Commentaries on the Constitution of the United States,” pp. 85-115.]
b [ Congress made this declaration on February 21, 1787.]
c [ It consisted of fifty-five members; Washington, Madison, Hamilton, and the two Morrises were amongst the number.]
d [ It was not adopted by the legislative bodies, but representatives were elected by the people for this sole purpose; and the new constitution was discussed at length in each of these assemblies.]
Summary of the Federal Constitution
Division of authority between the Federal Government and the States — The Government of the States is the rule, the Federal Government the exception.

The first question that awaited the Americans was intricate and by no means easy to solve. The aim was to divide the authority of the different States that made up the Union in such a way that each would continue to govern itself in everything concerning its internal prosperity, while the entire nation, represented by the Union, would continue to form a compact body and provide for the general needs of the people. It was as impossible to determine in advance, with any degree of accuracy, the share of authority each of the two governments was to enjoy, as to foresee all the incidents in the existence of a nation.

The obligations and claims of the Federal Government were simple and easily definable, because the Union had been formed with the express purpose of meeting the general needs of the people. The claims and obligations of the States, on the other hand, were complicated and varied, because those Governments had penetrated into all the details of social life. The attributes of the Federal Government were therefore carefully enumerated, and all that was not included among them was declared to belong to the privileges of the several State Governments. Thus the government of the States remained the rule, and that of the Confederation became the exception. *e
e [ See the Amendment to the Federal Constitution; “Federalist,” No. 32; Story, p. 711; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 364.

It should be noted that whenever the Constitution does not reserve the exclusive right of regulating certain matters to Congress, the States may take up the affair until it is brought before the National Assembly. For instance, Congress has the right to make a general bankruptcy law, but has neglected to do so. Each State is then free to make a law for itself. This point has been settled through litigation in the courts, and may be said to belong more properly to jurisprudence.]

But it was foreseen that, in practice, questions might arise as to the exact limits of this exceptional authority, and that it would be dangerous to submit such questions to the ordinary courts established in the States by the States themselves. A high Federal court was therefore created, *f whose task, among other functions, was to maintain the balance of power the Constitution had established between the two rival Governments. *g
f [ The action of this court is indirect, as we shall hereafter show.]

g [ This is how “The Federalist,” No. 45, explains the division of supremacy between the Union and the States: “The powers delegated by the Constitution to the Federal Government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State Governments are numerous and indefinite. The former will be exercised principally on external objects, as war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce. The powers reserved to the several States will extend to all the objects which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the internal order and prosperity of the State.” I shall often have occasion to quote “The Federalist” in this work. When the bill that later became the Constitution of the United States was submitted for the people’s approval, and while discussions were still pending, three men who had already earned part of the celebrity they would later enjoy — John Jay, Hamilton, and Madison — formed an association with the intention of explaining to the nation the advantages of the measure being proposed. With this view they published a series of articles in the form of a journal, which now form a complete treatise. They entitled their journal “The Federalist,” a name retained in the book. “The Federalist” is an excellent work, which ought to be familiar to the statesmen of all countries, although it especially concerns America.]
Prerogative of the Federal Government

Power of declaring war, making peace, and levying general taxes vested in the Federal Government — What part of the internal policy of the country it may direct — The Government of the Union is in some respects more centralized than the King’s Government in the old French monarchy.

The external relations of a people may be compared to those of private individuals, and they cannot be managed to advantage without the agency of a single head of government. The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and of equipping fleets was granted to the Union. *h The need for a national Government was less strongly felt in the conduct of the country’s internal policy, but there are certain general interests that can only be served advantageously by a general authority. The Union was vested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads that were to establish communication between the different parts of the country. *i The independence of each State’s Government within its own sphere was formally recognized; nevertheless, the Federal Government was authorized to intervene in the internal affairs of the States *j in a few predetermined cases, where an imprudent abuse of their independence might compromise the security of the Union as a whole. Thus, while the power of modifying and changing their legislation at will was preserved in all the republics, they were forbidden to enact ex post facto laws or to create a class of nobles within their communities. *k Finally, since the Federal Government had to be able to fulfill its obligations, it was endowed with an unlimited power of levying taxes. *l
h [ See Constitution, sect. 8; “Federalist,” Nos. 41 and 42; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 207; Story, pp. 358-382; Ibid. pp. 409-426.]

i [ Several other privileges of the same kind exist, such as that which empowers the Union to legislate on bankruptcy, to grant patents, and other matters in which its intervention is clearly necessary.]
j [ Even in these cases its interference is indirect. The Union interferes by means of the tribunals, as will be hereafter shown.]
k [ Federal Constitution, sect. 10, art. I.]
l [ Constitution, sects. 8, 9, and 10; “Federalist,” Nos. 30-36, inclusive, and 41-44; Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. pp. 207 and 381; Story, pp. 329 and 514.]

In examining the balance of power established by the Federal Constitution — noting on one hand the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States, and on the other the share of power the Union has assumed — it is clear that the Federal legislators held the most accurate notions on the nature of governmental centralization. The United States form not only a republic, but a confederation; nevertheless, the authority of the nation is more centralized than it was in several of the monarchies of Europe when the American Constitution was framed. Take, for instance, the following two examples.

Thirteen supreme courts of justice existed in France, which, generally speaking, had the right to interpret the law without appeal, and those provinces known as pays d’états were authorized to refuse their assent to a tax levied by the sovereign who represented the nation. In the Union there is only one court to interpret, just as there is one legislature to make the laws, and a tax voted by the representatives of the nation is binding on all citizens. On these two essential points, therefore, the Union exercises more central authority than the French monarchy possessed, although the Union is only an assemblage of confederate republics.

In Spain, certain provinces had the right to establish their own customs duties, although that privilege by its very nature belongs to national sovereignty. In America, Congress alone has the right to regulate the commercial relations of the States. The government of the Confederation is therefore more centralized in this respect than the kingdom of Spain. It is true that the power of the Crown in France or in Spain could always obtain by force whatever the Constitution of the country denied, and that the ultimate result was consequently the same; but I am discussing here the theory of the Constitution.
Once the limits within which the Federal Government was to act had been settled, the next step was to determine the powers it was to exercise.
Legislative Powers *m
m [ [In this chapter the author points out the essence of the conflict between the seceding States and the Union which caused the Civil War of 1861.]]

Division of the Legislative Body into two branches — Difference in the manner of forming the two Houses — The principle of the independence of the States predominates in the formation of the Senate — The principle of the sovereignty of the nation in the composition of the House of Representatives — Singular effects of the fact that a Constitution can only be logical in the early stages of a nation.

The plan laid down beforehand for the Constitutions of the several States was followed on many points in the organization of the powers of the Union. The Federal legislature was composed of a Senate and a House of Representatives. A spirit of conciliation required that distinct principles be observed in the formation of these two assemblies. I have already shown that two opposite interests were at odds in the establishment of the Federal Constitution. These two interests had given rise to two opinions. One party wanted to turn the Union into a league of independent States, or a kind of congress at which the representatives of the several peoples would meet to discuss certain matters of common interest. The other party wanted to unite the inhabitants of the American colonies into a single nation, and to establish a Government that would act as the sole representative of the nation, as far as the limited sphere of its authority would permit. The practical consequences of these two theories were very different.

The question was whether a league was to be established instead of a national Government — whether the majority of the States, rather than the majority of the inhabitants of the Union, would make the law. In that case every State, small as well as large, would remain in full enjoyment of its independence and enter the Union on a footing of perfect equality. If, on the other hand, the inhabitants of the United States were to be considered as belonging to one and the same nation, it would be just that the majority of the citizens of the Union should prescribe the law. The smaller States could not subscribe to this doctrine without effectively abdicating their existence with respect to the sovereignty of the Confederation, since they would have passed from the condition of a co-equal and co-legislative authority to that of an insignificant fraction of a great people. If the former system would have invested them with excessive authority, the latter would have annulled their influence altogether. Under these circumstances, the result was that the strict rules of logic were evaded — as usually happens when interests are opposed to arguments. The legislators hit upon a middle course that forcibly brought together two systems theoretically irreconcilable.

The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in the formation of the Senate, and the principle of the sovereignty of the nation prevailed in the composition of the House of Representatives. It was decided that each State should send two senators to Congress, and a number of representatives proportional to its population. *n As a result of this arrangement, the State of New York today has forty representatives and only two senators, while the State of Delaware has two senators and only one representative. Delaware is therefore equal to New York in the Senate, while New York has forty times Delaware’s influence in the House of Representatives. Thus, if the minority of the nation happens to prevail in the Senate, it may paralyze the decisions of the majority represented in the other House — which is contrary to the spirit of constitutional government.

n [ Every ten years Congress fixes anew the number of representatives which each State is to furnish. The total number was 69 in 1789, and 240 in 1833. (See “American Almanac,” 1834, p. 194.) The Constitution decided that there should not be more than one representative for every 30,000 persons; but no minimum was fixed on. The Congress has not thought fit to augment the number of representatives in proportion to the increase of population. The first Act which was passed on the subject (April 14, 1792: see “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 235) decided that there should be one representative for every 33,000 inhabitants. The last Act, which was passed in 1832, fixes the proportion at one for 48,000. The population represented is composed of all the free men and of three-fifths of the slaves.

[The last Act of apportionment, passed February 2, 1872, fixes the representation at one to 134,684 inhabitants. There are now (1875) 283 members of the lower House of Congress, and 9 for the States at large, making in all 292 members. The old States have of course lost the representatives which the new States have gained.—Translator’s Note.]]

These facts show how rare and how difficult it is to combine all the several parts of legislation in a rational and logical way. In the course of time, different interests arise and different principles are sanctioned by the same people; and when a general constitution is to be established, these interests and principles are so many natural obstacles to the rigorous application of any political system in all its consequences. The early stages of national existence are the only periods at which the complete logic of legislation can be maintained. When we see a nation enjoying this advantage, before we hasten to conclude that it is wise, we would do well to remember that it is young. When the Federal Constitution was formed, the interest of independence for the separate States and the interest of union for the whole people were the only two conflicting interests among the Anglo-Americans, and a compromise had to be made between them.

It is only fair to acknowledge, however, that this part of the Constitution has not so far produced the evils that might have been feared. All the States are young and contiguous; their customs, their ideas, and their needs are not dissimilar; and the differences that arise from their size do not suffice to set their interests at odds. The small States have therefore never been induced to league together in the Senate to oppose the designs of the larger ones. Indeed, there is so irresistible an authority in the legitimate expression of the will of a people that the Senate could offer only feeble resistance to the vote of the majority of the House of Representatives.

It must not be forgotten, on the other hand, that the American legislators could not reduce the people for whom they were making laws to a single nation. The object of the Federal Constitution was not to destroy the independence of the States but to restrain it. By acknowledging the real authority of these secondary communities (and it was impossible to deprive them of it), they disavowed in advance the habitual use of force to enforce the decisions of the majority. On this principle, the introduction of the States’ influence into the mechanism of the Federal Government was not at all surprising, since it only attested to the existence of a recognized power that had to be managed rather than forcibly checked.
A Further Difference Between the Senate and the House of Representatives

The Senate named by the provincial legislatures, the Representatives by the people — Double election of the former; single election of the latter — Term of the different offices — Peculiar functions of each House.

The Senate not only differs from the other House in the principle it represents, but also in the mode of its election, in the term for which it is chosen, and in the nature of its functions. The House of Representatives is chosen by the people, the Senate by the legislators of each State. The former is elected directly; the latter is elected by an elected body. The term for which representatives are chosen is only two years; that of senators is six. The functions of the House of Representatives are purely legislative, and the only share it takes in the judicial power is the impeachment of public officers. The Senate cooperates in the work of legislation, and tries those political offenses the House of Representatives submits to its decision. It also acts as the great executive council of the nation: the treaties concluded by the President must be ratified by the Senate, and the appointments he makes must be definitively approved by the same body. *o
o [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 52-56, inclusive; Story, pp. 199-314; Constitution of the United States, sects. 2 and 3.] The Executive Power *p
p [ See “The Federalist,” Nos. 67-77; Constitution of the United States, art. 2; Story, p. 315, pp. 615-780; Kent’s “Commentaries,” p. 255.]

Dependence of the President — He is elective and responsible — He is free to act within his own sphere under the inspection, but not under the direction, of the Senate — His salary fixed at his entry into office — Suspensive veto.

The American legislators undertook a difficult task in attempting to create an executive power dependent on the majority of the people, and yet strong enough to act without restraint within its own sphere. It was indispensable to the maintenance of the republican form of government that the representative of the executive power should be subject to the will of the nation.

The President is an elective magistrate. His honor, his property, his liberty, and his life are the securities the people has for the temperate use of his power. But in exercising his authority he cannot be called perfectly independent: the Senate takes cognizance of his relations with foreign powers and of the distribution of public appointments, so that he can neither be bribed nor employ the means of corruption. The legislators of the Union recognized that the executive power would be unable to fulfill its task with dignity and usefulness unless it enjoyed a greater degree of stability and strength than had been granted to it in the separate States.

The President is chosen for four years and may be reelected, so that the prospect of a prolonged administration may inspire him with hopeful undertakings for the public good and with the means of carrying them out. The President was made the sole representative of the executive power of the Union, and care was taken not to make his decisions subordinate to the vote of a council — a dangerous measure that tends both to clog the action of the Government and to diminish its responsibility. The Senate has the right to annul certain acts of the President, but it cannot compel him to take any action, nor does it share in the exercise of executive power.

The action of the legislature on the executive power may be direct, and we have just shown that the Americans carefully forestalled this influence; but it may also be indirect. Public assemblies that have the power of depriving an officer of state of his salary encroach on his independence, and since they are free to make the laws, it is to be feared that they may gradually appropriate to themselves part of the authority the Constitution vested in his hands. This dependence of the executive power is one of the defects inherent in republican constitutions. The Americans have not been able to counteract the tendency of legislative assemblies to take possession of the government, but they have rendered it less irresistible. The President’s salary is fixed, at the time of his entering office, for the whole period of his magistracy. The President is moreover provided with a suspensive veto, which allows him to oppose the passing of laws that might destroy the share of independence the Constitution gives him. The struggle between the President and the legislature must always be an unequal one, since the latter is sure to bear down all resistance by persevering in its plans. But the suspensive veto at least forces it to reconsider the matter, and if the motion is pressed forward, it must be backed by a two-thirds majority of the whole house. The veto is in effect a kind of appeal to the people. The executive power, which without this safeguard might have been secretly oppressed, uses this means to plead its cause and state its reasons. If it is objected that the legislature is certain to overpower all resistance by persevering in its plans, I reply that in the constitutions of every nation, whatever their kind, there exists a certain point at which the legislator is obliged to rely on the good sense and the virtue of his fellow citizens. This point is more visible and more easily found in republics, while it is more remote and more carefully concealed in monarchies, but it always exists somewhere. There is no country in the world where everything can be provided for by the laws, or where political institutions can serve as a substitute for common sense and public morality.
Differences Between the Position of the President of the United States and That of a Constitutional King of France

Executive power in the Northern States as limited and partial as the supremacy it represents — Executive power in France as universal as the supremacy it represents — The King a branch of the legislature — The President the mere executor of the law — Other differences resulting from the duration of the two powers — The President checked in the exercise of the executive authority — The King independent in its exercise — Notwithstanding these discrepancies, France is more akin to a republic than the Union is to a monarchy — Comparison of the number of public officers depending upon the executive power in the two countries.

The executive power has so important an influence on the destinies of nations that I am inclined to pause for a moment on this part of my subject, to explain more clearly the role it plays in America. To form an accurate idea of the position of the President of the United States, it may be useful to compare it with that of one of the constitutional kings of Europe. In this comparison I shall pay little attention to the outward signs of power, which are more likely to deceive the observer’s eye than to guide his inquiry. When a monarchy is gradually transformed into a republic, the executive power retains the titles, the honors, the etiquette, and even the funds of royalty long after its authority has disappeared. The English, having cut off the head of one king and driven another from his throne, were accustomed to approach the successor of those princes on their knees. On the other hand, when a republic falls under the sway of a single individual, the bearing of the sovereign is simple and unpretending, as if his authority were not yet paramount. When the emperors exercised unlimited control over the fortunes and lives of their fellow citizens, they were customarily called Caesar in conversation, and had the habit of supping informally at their friends’ houses. It is therefore necessary to look below the surface.

The sovereignty of the United States is divided between the Union and the States, while in France it is undivided and compact. From this arises the first and most notable difference between the President of the United States and the King of France. In the United States, the executive power is as limited and partial as the sovereignty of the Union in whose name it acts; in France, it is as universal as the authority of the State. The Americans have a federal Government, the French a national Government.

This cause of inferiority arises from the nature of things, but it is not the only one. The second in importance is as follows. Sovereignty may be defined as the right of making laws. In France the King really exercises a portion of the sovereign power, since laws have no force until he has given his assent; he is, moreover, the executor of all they ordain. The President is also the executor of the laws, but he does not really take part in their formation, since the refusal of his assent does not annul them. He is therefore to be considered merely as the agent of the sovereign power. But not only does the King of France exercise a share of the sovereign power, he also helps nominate the legislature that exercises the other share. He has the privilege of appointing the members of one chamber and of dissolving the other at his pleasure, whereas the President of the United States has no share in the formation of the legislative body and cannot dissolve any part of it. The King has the same right of bringing forward measures as the Chambers — a right the President does not possess. The King is represented in each assembly by his ministers, who explain his intentions, support his opinions, and maintain the principles of the Government. The President and his ministers are alike excluded from Congress, so that his influence and opinions can only penetrate that great body indirectly. The King of France therefore stands on an equal footing with the legislature, which can no more act without him than he without it. The President exercises an authority that is inferior to, and dependent upon, that of the legislature.

Even in the exercise of the executive power properly so called — the point on which his position seems most analogous to that of the King of France — the President labors under several causes of inferiority. The authority of the King, in France, has, in the first place, the advantage of duration over that of the President, and durability is one of the chief elements of strength; nothing is either loved or feared but what is likely to endure. The President of the United States is a magistrate elected for four years; the King of France is a hereditary sovereign. In the exercise of the executive power, the President of the United States is constantly subject to a jealous scrutiny. He may make, but he cannot conclude, a treaty; he may designate, but he cannot appoint, a public officer. *q The King of France is absolute within the limits of his authority. The President of the United States is responsible for his actions, but the person of the King is declared inviolable by the French Charter. *r

q [ The Constitution had left it doubtful whether the President was obliged to consult the Senate in the removal as well as in the appointment of Federal officers. “The Federalist” (No. 77) seemed to establish the affirmative; but in 1789 Congress formally decided that, as the President was responsible for his actions, he ought not to be forced to employ agents who had forfeited his esteem. See Kent’s “Commentaries”, vol. i. p. 289.]
r [ [This comparison applied to the Constitutional King of France and to the powers he held under the Charter of 1830, till the overthrow of the monarchy in 1848.—Translator’s Note.]]

Nevertheless, the supremacy of public opinion is no less above the head of the one than of the other. This power is less definite, less evident, and less sanctioned by the laws in France than in America, but it exists in fact. In America it acts through elections and decrees; in France it proceeds by revolutions; but notwithstanding the different constitutions of these two countries, public opinion is the dominant authority in both. The fundamental principle of legislation — a principle essentially republican — is the same in both countries, although its consequences may be different and its results more or less extensive. From this I am led to conclude that France with its King is more akin to a republic than the Union with its President is to a monarchy.

In what I have said so far I have only touched on the main points of distinction; if I could have gone into details, the contrast would have been even more striking. I have observed that the authority of the President in the United States is exercised only within the limits of a partial sovereignty, while that of the King in France is undivided. I could go on to show that the power of the King’s government in France exceeds its natural limits, extensive as they are, and penetrates in a thousand ways into the administration of private interests. Among the examples of this influence one may cite the great number of public functionaries, all of whom derive their appointments from the Government. This number now exceeds all previous limits: it amounts to 138,000 *s nominations, each of which may be considered an element of power. The President of the United States does not have the exclusive right of making public appointments, and their whole number scarcely exceeds 12,000. *t
s [ The sums annually paid by the State to these officers amount to 200,000,000 fr. ($40,000,000).]

t [ This number is extracted from the “National Calendar” for 1833. The “National Calendar” is an American almanac which contains the names of all the Federal officers. It results from this comparison that the King of France has eleven times as many places at his disposal as the President, although the population of France is not much more than double that of the Union.

[I have not the means of ascertaining the number of appointments now at the disposal of the President of the United States, but his patronage and the abuse of it have largely increased since 1833.—Translator’s Note, 1875.]]
Accidental Causes Which May Increase the Influence of the Executive Government
External security of the Union — Army of six thousand men — Few ships — The President has no opportunity of exercising his great prerogatives — In the prerogatives he exercises he is weak.
If the executive government is feebler in America than in France, the cause lies more in circumstances than in the laws of the country.

It is chiefly in its foreign relations that the executive power of a nation is called on to exert its skill and its vigor. If the existence of the Union were perpetually threatened, and if its chief interests were in daily contact with those of other powerful nations, the executive government would gain an importance proportional to what was expected of it and what it would carry into effect. The President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the army, but of an army of only six thousand men. He commands the fleet, but the fleet has few ships. He conducts the foreign relations of the Union, but the United States are a nation without neighbors. Separated from the rest of the world by the ocean, and as yet too weak to aim at dominion over the seas, they have no enemies, and their interests rarely come into contact with those of any other nation on earth.

The practical workings of a Government must not be judged by the theory of its constitution. The President of the United States possesses almost royal prerogatives that he has no opportunity to exercise, and the privileges he can actually use are very narrow. The laws allow him an influence that circumstances do not permit him to employ.

On the other hand, the great strength of the royal prerogative in France comes from circumstances far more than from the laws. There the executive government is constantly struggling against enormous obstacles and exerting all its energies to keep them down, so that it grows by the extent of its achievements and by the importance of the events it controls, without any modification of its constitution. If the laws had made it as feeble and as narrow as in the Union, its influence would very soon become still more preponderant.

Why the President of the United States Does Not Require the Majority of the Two Houses in Order to Carry On the Government — It is an established axiom in Europe that a constitutional King cannot persevere in a system of government opposed by the two other branches of the legislature. But several Presidents of the United States have been known to lose the majority in the legislative body without being obliged to give up the supreme power, and without inflicting any serious evil on society. I have heard this fact cited as an instance of the independence and power of the executive government in America; a moment’s reflection will convince us, on the contrary, that it is a proof of its extreme weakness.

A King in Europe needs the support of the legislature to carry out the duties imposed on him by the Constitution, because those duties are enormous. A constitutional King in Europe is not merely the executor of the law; the execution of its provisions falls so completely upon him that he has the power to paralyze its effect if it crosses his designs. He needs the help of the legislative assemblies to make the law, but those assemblies need his aid to execute it. These two authorities cannot subsist without each other, and the mechanism of government comes to a halt as soon as they are at odds.

In America the President cannot prevent any law from being passed, nor can he evade the obligation to enforce it. His sincere and zealous cooperation is no doubt useful, but it is not indispensable to the conduct of public affairs. All his important acts are directly or indirectly submitted to the legislature, and on his own authority he can do very little. It is therefore his weakness, not his power, that enables him to remain in opposition to Congress. In Europe, harmony must reign between the Crown and the other branches of the legislature, because a collision between them may prove serious; in America, this harmony is not indispensable, because such a collision is impossible.
Election of the President

Dangers of the elective system increase in proportion to the extent of the prerogative — This system possible in America because no powerful executive authority is required — What circumstances are favorable to the elective system — Why the election of the President does not cause a deviation from the principles of the Government — Influence of the election of the President on secondary functionaries.

The dangers of the elective system applied to the head of the executive government of a great people have been sufficiently shown by experience and by history, and the remarks I am about to make refer to America alone. These dangers may be more or less formidable in proportion to the place the executive power occupies and to the importance it has in the State, and they may vary according to the mode of election and the circumstances of the electors. The weightiest argument against the election of a chief magistrate is that it offers so splendid a lure to private ambition, and is so apt to inflame men in the pursuit of power, that when legitimate means are lacking, force may often seize what right denied.

Clearly, the greater the privileges of the executive authority, the greater the temptation. The more the ambition of the candidates is inflamed, the more warmly their interests are espoused by a throng of partisans who hope to share the power when their patron has won the prize. The dangers of the elective system therefore increase in exact proportion to the influence the executive power exercises in the affairs of State. The revolutions of Poland were not attributable to the elective system in general alone, but to the fact that the elected monarch was the sovereign of a powerful kingdom. Before we can discuss the absolute advantages of the elective system, we must first inquire whether the geographical position, the laws, the habits, the manners, and the opinions of the people among whom it is to be introduced will permit the establishment of a weak and dependent executive government. To try to render the representative of the State a powerful sovereign and at the same time elective is, in my opinion, to pursue two incompatible aims. To reduce hereditary royalty to the condition of an elective authority, the only means I know are to circumscribe its sphere of action beforehand, gradually to diminish its prerogatives, and to accustom the people to live without its protection. Nothing, however, is further from the designs of the republicans of Europe than this course. Since many of them owe their hatred of tyranny to the sufferings they have personally undergone, it is oppression — and not the extent of the executive power — that provokes their hostility, and they attack the former without seeing how closely it is connected with the latter.

So far, no citizen has shown any disposition to risk his honor and his life in order to become the President of the United States, because the power of that office is temporary, limited, and subordinate. The prize of fortune must be great to tempt adventurers into so desperate a game. No candidate has yet been able to rouse the dangerous enthusiasm or the passionate sympathies of the people in his favor, for the very simple reason that when he is at the head of the Government, he has but little power, little wealth, and little glory to share among his friends; and his influence in the State is too small for the success or the ruin of a faction to depend on the elevation of an individual to power.

The great advantage of hereditary monarchies is that, since the private interest of a family is always intimately bound up with the interests of the State, the executive government is never suspended for a single instant. And if the affairs of a monarchy are not better managed than those of a republic, at least there is always someone to manage them, well or ill, according to his capacity. In elective States, by contrast, the wheels of government cease to turn, as it were, of their own accord as an election approaches, and even for some time before it. Laws may indeed accelerate the operation of the election, which may be conducted with such simplicity and speed that the seat of power is never left vacant; but despite these precautions, a break inevitably occurs in the minds of the people.

As an election approaches, the head of the executive government is wholly taken up with the coming struggle; his future plans are in doubt; he can undertake nothing new, and he will only prosecute with indifference those designs that another may have to finish. “I am so near the time of my retirement from office,” said President Jefferson on the 21st of January, 1809 (six weeks before the election), “that I feel no passion, I take no part, I express no sentiment. It appears to me just to leave to my successor the commencement of those measures which he will have to prosecute, and for which he will be responsible.”

On the other side, the eyes of the nation are fixed on a single point; all are watching the gradual birth of so important an event. The wider the influence of the executive power extends, the greater and the more necessary its constant action, the more fatal this period of suspense becomes. A nation accustomed to the government — still more, one used to the administrative protection of a powerful executive authority — would infallibly be convulsed by an election of this kind. In the United States, the action of the Government can be slackened with impunity, because it is always weak and narrowly limited. *u

u [ [This, however, may be a great danger. The period during which Mr. Buchanan retained office, after the election of Mr. Lincoln, from November, 1860, to March, 1861, was that which enabled the seceding States of the South to complete their preparations for the Civil War, and the Executive Government was paralyzed. No greater evil could befall a nation.—Translator’s Note.]]

One of the principal vices of the elective system is that it always introduces a certain degree of instability into the internal and external policy of the State. But this disadvantage is less keenly felt if the share of power vested in the elected magistrate is small. In Rome the principles of the Government underwent no variation, although the Consuls were changed every year, because the Senate, which was a hereditary assembly, held the directing authority. If the elective system were adopted in Europe, the condition of most monarchical States would change at every new election. In America the President exercises a certain influence on State affairs, but he does not conduct them; the preponderant power lies with the representatives of the whole nation. The political maxims of the country therefore depend on the mass of the people, not on the President alone, and consequently in America the elective system has no very harmful influence on the fixed principles of the Government. But the lack of fixed principles is an evil so inherent in the elective system that it is still extremely perceptible even within the narrow sphere to which the President’s authority extends.

The Americans have accepted that the head of the executive power, who bears the whole responsibility of the duties he is called on to fulfill, ought to be empowered to choose his own agents and to remove them at pleasure. The legislative bodies watch the conduct of the President more than they direct it. The consequence is that at every new election the fate of all the Federal public officers hangs in the balance. Mr. Quincy Adams, on entering office, dismissed the majority of those appointed by his predecessor; and I am not aware that General Jackson allowed a single removable functionary employed in the Federal service to retain his place beyond the first year after his election. It is sometimes complained that in the constitutional monarchies of Europe the fate of the humbler servants of an Administration depends on that of the Ministers. But in elective Governments this evil is far greater. In a constitutional monarchy, successive ministries are formed quickly, but since the principal representative of the executive power does not change, the spirit of innovation is kept within bounds. The changes that take place are in the details rather than in the principles of the administrative system. But to substitute one system for another, as is done in America every four years by law, is to cause a kind of revolution. As for the hardships that may fall on individuals as a result, it must be admitted that the uncertain situation of the public officers carries fewer bad consequences in America than elsewhere. It is so easy to acquire an independent position in the United States that the public officer who loses his place may be deprived of the comforts of life, but not of the means of subsistence.

I remarked at the beginning of this chapter that the dangers of the elective system applied to the head of the State are increased or diminished by the particular circumstances of the people that adopts it. However restricted the functions of the executive power may be, it must always exert great influence on the country’s foreign policy, since a negotiation cannot be opened or successfully carried on other than by a single agent. The more precarious and perilous a people’s position becomes, the more absolute the need for a fixed and consistent foreign policy, and the more dangerous the elective system for the Chief Magistrate becomes. The policy of the Americans in relation to the rest of the world is exceedingly simple: it may almost be said that no country stands in need of them, nor do they need the cooperation of any other people. Their independence is never threatened. In their present condition, then, the functions of the executive power are no less limited by circumstances than by the laws, and the President can often change his line of policy without involving the State in difficulty or ruin.

Whatever the prerogatives of the executive power, the period immediately before an election and the period of its duration must always be considered a national crisis, one whose peril is proportional to the country’s internal embarrassments and external dangers. Few of the nations of Europe could escape the calamities of anarchy or conquest every time they had to elect a new sovereign. In America society is so constituted that it can stand on its own foundation without assistance; nothing is to be feared from the pressure of external dangers, and the election of the President is a cause of agitation but not of ruin.

Besides the dangers inherent in the system itself, many other difficulties may arise from the mode of election, which the legislator’s prudence can forestall. When a people met in arms in some public spot to choose its head, it was exposed to all the chances of civil war resulting from so martial a procedure, in addition to the dangers of the elective system itself. The Polish laws, which subjected the election of the sovereign to the veto of a single individual, suggested either the murder of that individual or prepared the way for anarchy.

In examining the institutions and the political as well as social condition of the United States, we are struck by the admirable harmony between the gifts of fortune and the efforts of man. The nation possessed two of the main causes of internal peace: it was a new country, but it was inhabited by a people grown old in the exercise of freedom. America had no hostile neighbors to fear. Profiting by these favorable circumstances, the American legislators created a weak and subordinate executive power that could be made elective without danger.

It only remained for them to choose the least dangerous of the various modes of election, and the rules they laid down on this point correspond admirably to the securities the country’s physical and political constitution already provided. Their aim was to find the mode of election that would best express the choice of the people with the least possible excitement and suspense. It was accepted first of all that the simple majority should be decisive; but the difficulty was to obtain this majority without the kind of delay it was most important to avoid. It rarely happens that a single individual can at once gather a majority of the votes of a great people, and this difficulty is heightened in a republic of confederate States, where local influences are apt to preponderate. The means proposed to overcome this second obstacle was to delegate the electoral powers of the nation to a body of representatives. This mode of election made a majority more probable, for the fewer the electors, the greater the chance of their reaching a final decision. It also offered a greater probability of a judicious choice. It then remained to be decided whether this right of election should be entrusted to a legislative body — the habitual representative assembly of the nation — or whether an electoral assembly should be formed expressly for the purpose of nominating a President. The Americans chose the latter alternative, believing that the individuals returned to make the laws were not competent to represent the wishes of the nation in the election of its chief magistrate, and that, since they are chosen for more than a year, the constituency they represent might have changed its opinion in that time. It was thought that if the legislature were empowered to elect the head of the executive power, its members would for some time before the election be exposed to the maneuvers of corruption and the tricks of intrigue, whereas the special electors would, like a jury, remain mixed with the crowd until the day of action, when they would appear for the sole purpose of casting their votes.

It was therefore established that every State should name a certain number of electors, *v who in turn should elect the President. And since it had been observed that the assemblies entrusted with the choice of a chief magistrate in elective countries inevitably became centers of passion and cabal; that they sometimes usurped an authority that did not belong to them; and that their proceedings, or the uncertainty they produced, were sometimes prolonged so long as to endanger the welfare of the State — it was decided that the electors should all vote on the same day, without being convened in the same place. *w This double election made a majority probable, though not certain, for as many differences might exist among the electors as among their constituents. In such a case, one of three measures would have to be resorted to: either to appoint new electors, to consult once again those already appointed, or to defer the election to another authority. The first two alternatives, apart from the uncertainty of their results, were likely to delay the final decision and to prolong an agitation that must always be accompanied with danger. The third expedient was therefore adopted, and it was agreed that the votes should be transmitted sealed to the President of the Senate, and that they should be opened and counted in the presence of the Senate and the House of Representatives. If no candidate has a majority, the House of Representatives immediately proceeds to elect a President, on condition that it choose one of the three candidates with the highest numbers. *x
v [ As many as it sends members to Congress. The number of electors at the election of 1833 was 288. (See “The National Calendar,” 1833.)]

w [ The electors of the same State assemble, but they transmit to the central government the list of their individual votes, and not the mere result of the vote of the majority.] [Footnote x: In this case it is the majority of the States, and not the majority of the members, which decides the question; so that New York has not more influence in the debate than Rhode Island. Thus the citizens of the Union are first consulted as members of one and the same community; and, if they cannot agree, recourse is had to the division of the States, each of which has a separate and independent vote. This is one of the singularities of the Federal Constitution which can only be explained by the jar of conflicting interests.]

Thus it is only in the event of something that cannot happen often, and can never be foreseen, that the election is entrusted to the ordinary representatives of the nation. And even then they are obliged to choose a citizen who has already been designated by a powerful minority of the special electors. It is by this happy expedient that respect for the popular voice is combined with the utmost speed of execution and with those precautions the peace of the country demands. But the decision of the question by the House of Representatives does not necessarily offer an immediate solution, for the majority of that assembly may still be in doubt, and in that case the Constitution prescribes no remedy. Nevertheless, by restricting the number of candidates to three, and by referring the matter to the judgment of an enlightened public body, it has smoothed away all the obstacles *y not inherent in the elective system itself.
y [ Jefferson, in 1801, was not elected until the thirty-sixth time of balloting.]

In the forty-four years since the promulgation of the Federal Constitution, the United States have chosen a President twelve times. Ten of these elections took place simultaneously by the votes of the special electors in the different States. The House of Representatives has only twice exercised its conditional privilege of deciding in cases of uncertainty: the first was at the election of Mr. Jefferson in 1801; the second was in 1825, when Mr. Quincy Adams was named. *z
z [ [General Grant is now (1874) the eighteenth President of the United States.]]
Crises of the Election
The Election may be considered as a national crisis — Why? — Passions of the people — Anxiety of the President — Calm which succeeds the agitation of the election.

I have shown what circumstances favored the adoption of the elective system in the United States, and what precautions the legislators took to forestall its dangers. The Americans are habitually accustomed to all kinds of elections, and they know by experience the utmost degree of excitement compatible with security. The vast extent of the country and the dispersion of the inhabitants make a collision between parties less probable and less dangerous there than elsewhere. The political circumstances under which the elections have so far been carried on have presented no real embarrassments to the nation.

Nevertheless, the time of a presidential election in the United States may be considered a crisis in the affairs of the nation. The influence the President exercises on public business is no doubt feeble and indirect; but the choice of the President, which is of small importance to each individual citizen, concerns the citizens collectively, and however trifling an interest may be, it assumes great importance as soon as it becomes general. The President has few means of rewarding his supporters compared with the kings of Europe, but the offices at his disposal are numerous enough to interest, directly or indirectly, several thousand electors in his success. Political parties in the United States are led to rally around an individual in order to take a more tangible shape in the eyes of the crowd, and the name of the candidate for the Presidency is held up as the symbol and personification of their theories. For these reasons, parties are strongly motivated to win the election — not so much in view of the triumph of their principles under the auspices of the President-elect, as to show by the majority that elected him the strength of those who support those principles.

For a long time before the appointed day arrives, the election becomes the most important and all-consuming topic of discussion. The ardor of faction is redoubled, and every artificial passion the imagination can produce in the heart of a happy and peaceful land is stirred up and brought into the open. The President, on his side, is absorbed in the cares of self-defense. He no longer governs in the interest of the State but in the interest of his reelection; he does homage to the majority, and instead of checking its passions as his duty requires, he often courts its worst caprices. As the election approaches, the activity of intrigue and the agitation of the populace increase. The citizens divide into hostile camps, each taking the name of its favorite candidate; the whole nation glows with feverish excitement; the election is the daily theme of the public papers, the subject of private conversation, the goal of every thought and every action, the sole interest of the present. As soon as the choice is decided, this ardor is dispelled, and as a calmer season returns, the current of the State, which had nearly broken its banks, sinks back to its usual level: *a but who can help being astonished at the causes of the storm.

Re-election of the President

When the head of the executive power is reeligible, it is the State that becomes the source of intrigue and corruption — The desire of being reelected the chief aim of a President of the United States — Disadvantage of the system peculiar to America — The natural evil of democracy is that it subordinates all authority to the slightest desires of the majority — The re-election of the President encourages this evil.

It may be asked whether the legislators of the United States did right or wrong in allowing the reelection of the President. At first sight it seems contrary to all reason to prevent the head of the executive power from being elected a second time. The influence that the talents and character of a single individual may exercise on the fate of a whole people in critical circumstances or difficult times is well known. A law preventing the reelection of the chief magistrate would deprive the citizens of the surest pledge of the prosperity and security of the commonwealth. And by a singular inconsistency, a man would be excluded from the government at the very moment he had shown his ability to conduct its affairs.

But if these arguments are strong, perhaps still more powerful ones can be urged against them. Intrigue and corruption are the natural vices of elective government, but when the head of the State can be reelected, these evils rise to a great pitch and compromise the very existence of the country. When a simple candidate seeks to rise by intrigue, his maneuvers must necessarily be confined to a narrow sphere; but when the chief magistrate enters the field, he borrows the strength of the government for his own purposes. In the first case, the feeble resources of an individual are at work; in the second, the State itself, with all its immense influence, is busied in the work of corruption and cabal. The private citizen who uses the most immoral practices to gain power can only act in a way indirectly harmful to the public prosperity. But if the representative of the executive descends into the combat, the cares of government dwindle to second-rate importance, and the success of his election becomes his first concern. All the laws and all the negotiations he undertakes are to him nothing but electioneering schemes; offices become the reward of services rendered not to the nation but to its chief; and the influence of the government, if not injurious to the country, is at least no longer beneficial to the community for which it was created.

It is impossible to consider the ordinary course of affairs in the United States without noticing that the desire for reelection is the chief aim of the President, that his whole administration — even his most indifferent measures — tends to this object, and that as the crisis approaches, his personal interest takes the place of his interest in the public good. The principle of reeligibility renders the corrupt influence of elective government still more extensive and pernicious.

In America this principle exercises a peculiarly fatal influence on the sources of national existence. Every government seems afflicted by some evil inherent in its nature, and the genius of the legislator is shown in eluding its attacks. A State may survive the influence of a host of bad laws, and the mischief they cause is often exaggerated; but a law that encourages the growth of the canker within must prove fatal in the end, though its bad consequences may not be immediately perceived.

The principle of destruction in absolute monarchies lies in the excessive and unreasonable extension of the prerogative of the crown, and a measure tending to remove the constitutional provisions that counterbalance this influence would be radically bad, even if its immediate consequences were harmless. By the same reasoning, in countries governed by a democracy, where the people is constantly drawing all authority to itself, laws that increase or accelerate its action are direct assailants of the very principle of the government.

The greatest proof of the ability of the American legislators is that they clearly saw this truth and had the courage to act on it. They held that there had to be a certain authority above the body of the people which would enjoy a degree of independence without being entirely beyond popular control — an authority that would be forced to comply with the permanent determinations of the majority, but that could resist its caprices and refuse its most dangerous demands. To this end they concentrated the whole executive power of the nation in a single hand, granted extensive prerogatives to the President, and armed him with the veto to resist the encroachments of the legislature.

But by introducing the principle of reelection, they partly destroyed their own work; they made the President little inclined to exert the great power they had placed in his hands. If he were ineligible a second time, the President would be far from independent of the people, for his responsibility would not be lessened; but the favor of the people would not be so necessary to him as to induce him to court it by indulging its desires. If reeligible (and this is especially true today, when political morality is relaxed and great men are rare), the President of the United States becomes an easy tool in the hands of the majority. He adopts its likings and its animosities, he hastens to anticipate its wishes, he forestalls its complaints, he yields to its idlest cravings; instead of guiding it as the legislature intended, he is always ready to follow its bidding. Thus, in order not to deprive the State of an individual’s talents, those talents have been rendered almost useless; and to keep an expedient in reserve for extraordinary perils, the country has been exposed to daily dangers.

I have inquired into the legislative and executive power of the Union, and the judicial power now remains to be examined; but here I cannot conceal my fears from the reader. Their judicial institutions exercise a great influence on the condition of the Anglo-Americans, and they occupy a prominent place among what are properly called political institutions. In this respect they are peculiarly deserving of our attention. But I find it hard to explain the political role of the American tribunals without going into some technical details of their constitution and their forms of procedure — and I do not know how to descend to these minutiae without wearying the curiosity of the reader through the natural dryness of the subject, or without risking obscurity in a desire to be brief. I can hardly hope to escape these various evils, for if I appear too lengthy to a man of the world, a lawyer may on the other hand complain of my brevity. But these are the natural drawbacks of my subject, and especially of the point I am now about to discuss.

The great difficulty was not to devise the Constitution of the Federal Government, but to find a way of enforcing its laws. Governments generally have only two means of overcoming the opposition of the people they govern: the physical force at their disposal, and the moral force they derive from the decisions of the courts of justice.

A government that had no other means of exacting obedience than open war would be very near its ruin, for one of two things would likely happen: if its authority was slight and its character temperate, it would not resort to violence until the last extremity, and would connive at a number of partial acts of insubordination, in which case the State would gradually fall into anarchy; if it was enterprising and powerful, it would perpetually fall back on its physical strength and would quickly degenerate into a military despotism. Its activity, then, would be no less harmful to the community than its inaction.

The great end of justice is to substitute the notion of right for that of violence, and to place a legal barrier between the power of the government and the use of physical force. The authority that general opinion grants to the intervention of a court of justice is so surprisingly great that it clings to the mere formalities of justice, giving physical force to the shadow of the law. The moral force of the courts makes the introduction of physical force exceedingly rare and is very often substituted for it; and if physical force does prove indispensable, its power is doubled by the association of the idea of law.

A federal government stands in greater need of the support of judicial institutions than any other, because it is naturally weak and exposed to formidable opposition. *c If it were always obliged to resort to violence from the outset, it could not fulfill its task. The Union therefore needed a national judiciary to enforce the obedience of the citizens to its laws and to repel attacks that might be directed against them. The question then was which tribunals should exercise these privileges. Were they to be entrusted to the courts of justice already organized in every State? Or was it necessary to create federal courts? It can easily be shown that the Union could not adapt the judicial power of the States to its needs. The separation of the judiciary from the administrative power of the State no doubt affects the security of every citizen and the liberty of all. But it is no less important to the life of the nation that these several powers should have the same origin, follow the same principles, and act in the same sphere — in a word, that they should be correlative and homogeneous. No one, I presume, ever suggested the advantage of trying offenses committed in France by a foreign court of justice in order to secure the impartiality of the judges. The Americans form one people in relation to their Federal Government; but within this people, various political bodies have been allowed to subsist that are dependent on the national Government on a few points and independent on all the rest, each with a distinct origin, maxims of its own, and special means of conducting its affairs. To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals instituted by these political bodies would be to allow foreign judges to preside over the nation. And more than that: not only is each State foreign to the Union at large, but it is in perpetual opposition to common interests, since whatever authority the Union loses turns to the advantage of the States. Thus to enforce the laws of the Union by means of the tribunals of the States would be to allow not only foreign but partial judges to preside over the nation.

c [ Federal laws are those which most require courts of justice, and those at the same time which have most rarely established them. The reason is that confederations have usually been formed by independent States, which entertained no real intention of obeying the central Government, and which very readily ceded the right of command to the federal executive, and very prudently reserved the right of non-compliance to themselves.]

But the number of the State tribunals, even more than their character, rendered them unfit for the service of the nation. When the Federal Constitution was formed, there were already thirteen courts of justice in the United States deciding cases without appeal. That number has now grown to twenty-four. To suppose that a State can subsist when its fundamental laws may be subjected to twenty-four different interpretations at the same time is to advance a proposition contrary to both reason and experience.

The American legislators therefore agreed to create a federal judiciary to apply the laws of the Union and to decide certain questions affecting general interests, which were carefully determined in advance. The entire judicial power of the Union was concentrated in one tribunal, called the Supreme Court of the United States. But, to speed the dispatch of business, inferior courts were attached to it, empowered to decide cases of small importance without appeal, and with appeal the cases of greater magnitude. The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. To make them independent of the other authorities, their office was made inalienable, and it was decided that their salary, once fixed, could not be altered by the legislature. *d It was easy to proclaim the principle of a Federal judiciary, but difficulties multiplied when the extent of its jurisdiction had to be determined.

Means of Determining the Jurisdiction of the Federal Courts — Difficulty of determining the jurisdiction of separate courts of justice in confederations — The courts of the Union obtained the right of fixing their own jurisdiction — In what respect this rule attacks the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States — The sovereignty of these States restricted by the laws, and the interpretation of the laws — Consequently, the danger to the several States is more apparent than real.

Since the Constitution of the United States recognized two distinct powers facing each other, represented from a judicial standpoint by two distinct classes of courts, the utmost care in defining their separate jurisdictions would not have been enough to prevent frequent collisions between these tribunals. The question then arose: to whom was the right of deciding the competence of each court to be referred?

In nations that constitute a single body politic, when a question is debated between two courts concerning their mutual jurisdiction, a third tribunal is generally at hand to decide the difference, and this is achieved without difficulty, because in such nations questions of judicial competence have no connection with the privileges of the national supremacy. But it was impossible to create an arbiter between a superior court of the Union and the superior court of a separate State that would not belong to one of the two classes. It was therefore necessary to allow one of these courts to judge its own cause, and to take or retain cognizance of the contested point. To grant this privilege to the various courts of the States would have been to destroy the sovereignty of the Union in fact after having established it in law, for the interpretation of the Constitution would soon have restored to the States that portion of independence of which the terms of that act deprived them. The object of creating a Federal tribunal was to prevent the courts of the States from deciding questions affecting the national interests in their own department, and thus to form a uniform body of jurisprudence for the interpretation of the laws of the Union. This aim would not have been attained if the courts of the several States had been competent to decide in their separate capacities the cases from which they were obliged to abstain as Federal tribunals. The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore vested with the right to determine all questions of jurisdiction. *e

This was a severe blow to the independence of the States, which was now restricted not only by the laws but by the interpretation of them — by one limit that was known, and another that was ambiguous; by a rule that was certain, and a rule that was arbitrary. It is true that the Constitution had laid down the precise limits of the Federal supremacy; but whenever this supremacy is contested by one of the States, a Federal tribunal decides the question. Nevertheless, the dangers with which the independence of the States was threatened by this arrangement are less serious than they appeared. We shall see later that in America the real strength of the country lies in the provincial far more than in the Federal Government. The Federal judges are conscious of the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act, and they are more inclined to abandon a right of jurisdiction in cases where it is justly their own than to assert a privilege to which they have no legal claim.
Different Cases of Jurisdiction

The matter and the party are the first conditions of the Federal jurisdiction — Suits in which ambassadors are engaged — Suits of the Union — Of a separate State — By whom tried — Causes resulting from the laws of the Union — Why judged by the Federal tribunals — Causes relating to the performance of contracts tried by the Federal courts — Consequence of this arrangement.

Having appointed the means of fixing the competence of the Federal courts, the legislators of the Union defined the cases to fall within their jurisdiction. They established, on the one hand, that certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts without any regard to the particular nature of the cause; and on the other hand, that certain causes must always be brought before the same courts without any regard to the quality of the parties in the suit. These distinctions were therefore accepted as the basis of the Federal jurisdiction.

Ambassadors are the representatives of nations in a state of amity with the Union, and whatever concerns these persons concerns in some degree the whole Union. When an ambassador is a party to a suit, that suit affects the welfare of the nation, and a Federal tribunal is naturally called on to decide it.

The Union itself may be called into legal proceedings, and in such a case it would be contrary both to the customs of all nations and to common sense to appeal to a tribunal representing any sovereignty other than its own. The Federal courts therefore take cognizance of these affairs.

When two parties belonging to two different States are engaged in a suit, the case cannot properly be brought before a court of either State. The surest expedient is to choose a tribunal like that of the Union, which can arouse the suspicions of neither party, and which offers the most natural as well as the most certain remedy.

When the two parties are not private individuals but States, an important political consideration is added to the same motive of equity. The quality of the parties in this case gives a national importance to all their disputes, and the most trifling litigation of the States may be said to involve the peace of the whole Union. *f

f [ The Constitution also says that the Federal courts shall decide “controversies between a State and the citizens of another State.” And here a most important question of a constitutional nature arose, which was, whether the jurisdiction given by the Constitution in cases in which a State is a party extended to suits brought against a State as well as by it, or was exclusively confined to the latter. The question was most elaborately considered in the case of Chisholm v. Georgia, and was decided by the majority of the Supreme Court in the affirmative. The decision created general alarm among the States, and an amendment was proposed and ratified by which the power was entirely taken away, so far as it regards suits brought against a State.
